#### Jeff Atwood

21 Jan 2006
 — 2 min read
 — Comments

In Humanizing Peer Reviews, Karl Wiegers starts with a powerful pronouncement:

> Peer review – an activity in which people other than the author of a software deliverable examine it for defects and improvement opportunities – is one of the most powerful software quality tools available. Peer review methods include inspections, walkthroughs, peer desk checks, and other similar activities. After experiencing the benefits of peer reviews for nearly fifteen years, I would never work in a team that did not perform them.

After participating in code reviews for a while here at Vertigo, I believe that peer code reviews are the single biggest thing you can do to improve your code. If you’re not doing code reviews right now with another developer, you’re missing a lot of bugs in your code and cheating yourself out of some key professional development opportunities. As far as I’m concerned, my code isn’t done until I’ve gone over it with a fellow developer.

But don’t take my word for it. McConnell provides plenty of evidence for the efficacy of code reviews in Code Complete:

> ... software testing alone has limited effectiveness – the average defect detection rate is only 25 percent for unit testing, 35 percent for function testing, and 45 percent for integration testing. In contrast, the average effectiveness of design and code inspections are 55 and 60 percent. Case studies of review results have been impressive:

- In a software-maintenance organization, 55 percent of one-line maintenance changes were in error before code reviews were introduced. After reviews were introduced, only 2 percent of the changes were in error. When all changes were considered, 95 percent were correct the first time after reviews were introduced. Before reviews were introduced, under 20 percent were correct the first time.

- In a group of 11 programs developed by the same group of people, the first 5 were developed without reviews. The remaining 6 were developed with reviews. After all the programs were released to production, the first 5 had an average of 4.5 errors per 100 lines of code. The 6 that had been inspected had an average of only 0.82 errors per 100. Reviews cut the errors by over 80 percent.

- The Aetna Insurance Company found 82 percent of the errors in a program by using inspections and was able to decrease its development resources by 20 percent.

- IBM’s 500,000 line Orbit project used 11 levels of inspections. It was delivered early and had only about 1 percent of the errors that would normally be expected.

- A study of an organization at AT&T with more than 200 people reported a 14 percent increase in productivity and a 90 percent decrease in defects after the organization introduced reviews.

- Jet Propulsion Laboratories estimates that it saves about $25,000 per inspection by finding and fixing defects at an early stage.

The only hurdle to a code review is finding a developer you respect to do it, and making the time to perform the review. Once you get started, I think you’ll quickly find that every minute you spend in a code review is paid back tenfold.

If your organization is new to code reviews, I highly recommend Karl’s book, Peer Reviews in Software: A Practical Guide. The sample chapters Karl provides on his website are a great primer, too.

# How to review code effectively: A GitHub staff engineer’s philosophy

GitHub Staff Engineer Sarah Vessels discusses her philosophy of code review, what separates good code review from bad, her strategy for finding and reviewing code, and how to get the most from reviews of her own code.

Sarah Vessels·@cheshire137

July 23, 2024 

 
 |
 
 16 minutes

- Share:

As a staff engineer at GitHub, code review is one of my main focus areas in my day to day work. Over the past eight years, I’ve reviewed more than 7,000 pull requests. Why so many? Because code review is crucial to building good software and another set of eyes can often spot issues you would have otherwise missed.

I see code review as one of the most important aspects of my job. In fact, whenever I see that a teammate has a pull request ready for code review, I prefer to drop whatever branch I’m working on to review their proposed changes instead. After all, their pull request has already passed the continuous integration (CI) gauntlet and met the bar for their own judgment of “done,” so it’s probably closer to being shippable than my own in-progress work. I’d rather get their code over the finish line than churn an unknown amount of time more to finish my code.

The sooner I provide feedback — “This can be nil and cause an error,” “This looks like an n+1 query,” “It would be great to have a method signature on this” — the faster that feedback can be addressed and the bug squashed or feature shipped.

I’d like to share how I approach code review in hopes that we can all ship better code.

items.source:
## What is code review?

Strictly speaking, code reviews—via pull request reviews on GitHub—allow collaborators to comment on the changes proposed in pull requests, indicate their approval of the changes, or request further changes before the pull request is merged.

I see a pull request as the beginning of conversation. I read it as the author saying “I think this improves on what we have today.” Code review is a great opportunity to shape the product’s implementation. As a code reviewer, my job is to go back and forth in discussion with the author to improve their code by asking questions, questioning assumptions, and generally serving as a second set of eyes.

Why review code? It's good for your career

I’ve learned a great deal from other reviewers’ perspectives on my own code, and after repeated positive feedback thanking me for timely code reviews, I know that my code review comments have likewise helped level up my teammates. Put simply, code review has impact, and getting a promotion requires showing your impact.

Code reviews are impactful because they help exchange knowledge and increase shipping velocity. They are nice, linkable artifacts that peers and managers can use to show how helpful and knowledgeable you are. They can highlight good communication skills, particularly if there’s a complex or controversial change needed. So, making your case well in a code review can not only guide the product’s future and help stave off incidents, it can be good for your career.

## Fine-tune your code review process

items.source:
### How to find pull requests for review

I live in my GitHub notifications inbox. It’s one of just a few tabs I pin in my browser, so it’s always available. Any time I’m waiting on CI, I’m in between tasks, starting my day, or generally have a spare moment, I like to check my inbox. I find most of the pull requests I review there. Teams at GitHub tend to have a particular Slack channel they treat as home base, and that’s a good place to share ready-for-review pull requests—it’s one of the other main ways I discover pull requests.

I also have good luck using the GitHub Slack integration to subscribe a Slack channel to new pull requests relevant to my team. To filter which pull requests show up in Slack, I use a label specific to the team, then a ‘subscribe’ command in Slack like /github subscribe your/repo pulls +label:"your-team-label".

Tip

You can repeat the team-review-requested: qualifier in your query to get pull requests for review across many different code owners.

I like to search for outstanding pull requests that may need review with queries like is:open archived:false is:pr org:github -is:draft team-review-requested:github/relevant-codeowner-team. With that query, I find open, unarchived pull requests within the GitHub organization that are not drafts and have relevant codeowner teams as a requested reviewer. I usually will omit the review:required search qualifier because I’m interested in reviewing a pull request even if a teammate has already reviewed it. After all, reviewing code not only helps the author, it helps me stay up to date with changes affecting code I’m responsible for.

items.title: 如何高效评审代码
items.source:
### Use reviewer teams to manage notifications

You don’t want code changes to ping such a large team that everyone on the team assumes reviewing the change isn’t their responsibility. That can result in pull requests that either languish unreviewed or get merged before they should, because key reviewers missed them in a deluge of notifications. Both of these scenarios affect the quality of the product.

I recommend honing the number of code owner teams you’re on, if you’re able, to keep your notifications manageable. That way, pull requests that land in your inbox aren’t just noise, they’re actually something you feel you should review. While big, catch-all code owner teams can be okay as a fallback option, they aren’t great as a first-line default for automatic review requests. Keep your repository’s CODEOWNERS file well organized, with well-defined code boundaries to go along with it, to limit notifications and help reviewers avoid notification fatigue.

Another way of limiting team-based notifications is to create a first responders team and then use automation to add and remove team members based on a schedule. This can let your team focus on their day-to-day code base, while scheduled first responders get notified of pull requests in your team’s service areas. Using the PagerDuty API, for example, you can determine who is a first responder on a given day. You can then use the Octokit library to add and remove team members.

items.title: 如何高效评审代码
items.source:
### Standardize code reviews across teams with automation

Repository-level configuration and automation, such as using a CODEOWNERS file and branch protection rules, can be helpful to enforce review process standards across teams. Other standards, such as what’s worth commenting on in a pull request, have to be maintained by us humans. Document how code reviews work within your team to make sure anyone providing a code review or submitting a pull request knows how to get their pull requests reviewed, the expected turnaround time for review, and what automation is in use to facilitate review.

Some teams use a project board to keep track of which pull requests come in for review; I’ve seen this work well for a team that manages a shared API, an area often modified by those outside the team. Other teams depend on GitHub notifications alone, which I’ve seen work well when code ownership is tightly scoped and the team is disciplined about reviewing pull requests as they come in.

If you follow a process unique to your specific team, automation can help communicate expectations with those outside your team. For example, if many other teams depend on your team’s reviews, you can use a bot to automatically leave a comment on any pull request where your team’s review is requested, to tell the author when they can expect to hear from you.

items.source:
## What makes a code review good or bad?

Good code reviews add clarity and push code toward a better state than where it started.

As a reviewer, clarity in communication is key. You’ll want to make clear which of your comments are personal preference and which are blockers for approval. Provide an example of the approach you’re suggesting to elevate your code review and make your meaning even clearer. If you can provide an example from the same repository as the pull request, even better—that further supports your suggestion by encouraging consistent implementations.

By contrast, poor code reviews lack clarity. For example, a blanket approval or rejection without any comments can leave the pull request author wondering if the review was thorough. Even just reiterating your understanding of the pull request author’s intention with your approval can surface whether you and the author have the same understanding.

A code review that is unclear about when its suggestions should be implemented can also be a poor experience for the author. It’s fine to note that existing, unchanged code should be refactored, or an additional case should be handled, but it’s important to specify whether those are precursors to approval. If the pull request is okay to land without your suggestions, make sure to say so. It may be safer to keep a small diff and ship those changes separately, as separate pull requests.

Here’s a code review comment that displays specificity and clearly communicates suggested implementations:

“I see your new method matches the existing style in this file, taking [X] parameters. Having that many parameters hurts readability and implies the function is doing too much. What do you think about refactoring this method and the existing ones in a later pull request to reduce how many parameters they take?”

What this comment does well:

- Provides specific details.

- References specific code or issues.

- Suggests a resolution to the problem.

- Cites evidence or provides an explanation

On the other end of the spectrum, here are some examples of review comments that could be better:

“I don’t like this.” – What doesn’t the reviewer like? Do they have an alternative in mind that they could explicitly state?

Possible improvements:

- “This line is doing a lot, could we simplify it to improve readability?”

- “I think this will have performance problems because of an n+1 query.”

- “Could we use the [preferred framework]’s solution for this instead of writing a custom implementation?”

“This won’t work.” – Why won’t the changes work?

Possible improvements:

- “This won’t work because [X], see this relevant issue: [issue link].”

- “This was tried before in [pull request link] and it didn’t work because of [X].”

- “If you run into problems with [X], you could try [alternative approach] instead.”

“I think this fixes a bug.” – I love the callout, but is there any additional context, such as an issue link, that could make this more clear?

Possible improvements:

- “I think this fixes [issue link].”

- “Is this fixing the bug from [issue link]?”

- “This looks like the bug we ran into with [link to failing build]. Thanks for the fix!”

items.source: ## How to give a good code review

items.title: 如何高效评审代码
items.source:
### Ask questions

I think of the pull request author as the person with the most context on the changes their pull request is making. I can point out problems I see based on my history—my experience working in a Ruby on Rails monolith, in TypeScript, or with a database that gets a lot of traffic—but I trust the author’s answers to my questions. I treat their understanding of the particulars as better than mine.

Tip

If you’re new to a code base or team, ask questions in code reviews to learn about the tech stack and what internal tools and libraries are available. Every pull request you review is a chance to find out why the author preferred one approach to another.

I also love to ask questions that involve the assumptions made in the code. What is the shape of the data they’re working with? Does data exist that doesn’t match that shape? Does the code respond to that well? Is the code resource intensive? Will it perform well? As a reviewer, my favorite response is for the author to provide an automated test that verifies the behavior in those scenarios. My second favorite response is empirical data, such as a query from our data warehouse or a Datadog graph that shows why those scenarios aren’t a problem.

As a pull request author, I appreciate receiving questions. When someone asks a question, it makes space for me to explain why I’m confident about my change, citing issues, queries, or graphs as necessary. It also lets me share my knowledge and experience with others. The author not only sees my responses, but also other reviewers and future readers who may be tracking down context on a past decision.

items.title: 如何高效评审代码
items.source:
### Offer affirmations

Beyond asking questions, it’s good practice to comment on the parts of the pull request that you agree with. These comments can highlight that you read and understood what was being changed, or that you verified some assumption in the code. Here are a few examples:

- “Looks like this matches the pattern used in other classes in this module.”

- “Thanks for adding a test for this!”

- “This is much more readable than before.”

It’s also just nice being on the receiving end of such comments, in my experience. Receiving a code review can sometimes feel draining. When I’m fielding questions and suggestions from several parties, it can be a good boost to get a few comments that don’t ask anything of me and instead support and acknowledge the work I’ve already put in.

items.title: 如何高效评审代码
items.source:
### Be aware of biases and assumptions

It’s easy to let your biases about the reviewer, or the area of code they’re changing, affect your review. You get used to someone working in an area or having some level of seniority and assume they know what they’re doing—but everyone makes mistakes. Your eyes on their changes, your questions checking their assumptions or validating your own, can catch a problem before it’s deployed.

I’m big on writing tests because they take some of the bias out. When you write a test to check that code works properly, you don’t have to take the author’s word for it, you just look at whether the test passed—provided you get the test right, of course. 😅

I’m also big on junior developers asking senior developers questions in code review, even if they think their question is silly or has an obvious answer. If it’s not obvious to you, that’s valid. It won’t be obvious to someone else either! Ask the question, make the space for the author to write down their answer, and preserve that bit of education for those who come later.

items.title: 如何高效评审代码
items.source:
### To approve or not

I see my review as a blocking gate that can stop another person from improving our product, so I withhold approval conscientiously. I will often have personal preferences and suggest optional changes I’d like to see the author make, but I won’t withhold an approval based on those alone. If I have suggestions for someone’s pull request, but their pull request as it is won’t break production, negatively impact users, or otherwise cause problems, I will approve with those comments. The author can choose to address my feedback before they merge their pull request, or they can follow up in another branch.

Tip

Use feature flags and make your pull requests small. The less scary your change is, the faster it can be reversed in production, the easier it will be for me to approve it!

Keep in mind the importance of your suggestion when you’re reviewing code. Is it worth delaying the ship to get your suggestion addressed? Is it worth the whole cycle of the author seeing your feedback, making the suggested changes, waiting for CI, a re-review, deployment and finally merging? If a suggestion’s absence isn’t going to make someone’s day worse, let the author decide if or when to make the suggested change.

The ‘Request changes’ option stops a pull request from being merged until the reviewer comes back and approves it. I very rarely use it, as it usually feels too heavy-handed. I trust my team to know when to approve a pull request, so a teammate’s approval is fine in place of mine. Likewise, I trust the pull request author to respect my feedback and consider it, not just blindly merging because someone else approved but I didn’t. About the only time I’ll choose the ‘Request changes’ option is when I think there is an immediate security issue and I’m worried they won’t see my concern before merging.

Why code reviews matter when using AI coding tools

AI coding tools often include various safeguards against incorrect or insecure code, but don’t be lulled into a false sense of security. As the human reviewer at the helm, you are the last line of defense and should review all code with an equal level of diligence.

## How to get the most out of code reviews

items.source:
### Review your own code

GitHub Senior Software Engineer Paul Smith taught me to review my own pull request before asking others to do so, and I would advise you to do the same. Take a first pass and leave comments inline on non-obvious changes or ones you would ask about if you saw them in someone else’s pull request. A self-review can also help determine if a pull request is too big and would benefit from being split up.

Shout-out: if you care about keeping your pull requests small, you can make use of lerebear/sizeup-action to automatically apply a label to pull requests indicating their complexity and size.

items.title: 如何高效评审代码
items.source:
### Be welcoming of post-merge reviews

If I happen to merge a pull request before someone gets a chance to review it, I still welcome their review. If my pull request broke something or had unintended consequences, commenting as much on the pull request leaves that breadcrumb trail to help future readers track down what happened!

If I receive a review on a merged pull request, I’ll address the feedback like I would have before the pull request landed. Maybe that’ll be a comment to explain my perspective, maybe it’ll be additional pull requests to iterate on the code I originally shipped. Maybe it’ll be opening new issues to capture additional work to be done.

items.title: 如何高效评审代码
items.source:
### Use draft pull requests

When you create a new pull request, you have the option to set the pull request as a draft. I lean heavily on the draft stage to indicate whether or not I want reviews. For example, if a required CI build is failing or I’m just not finished yet, I’ll keep it as a draft. I tend to expect the same from others’ pull requests: if it’s a draft, I assume the author isn’t ready for reviews. If it’s marked as ready for review, I assume that getting enough approvals is all that’s preventing them from deploying the pull request.

The draft status implies that a pull request is not finished, so I move pull requests back to draft when resolving merge conflicts or addressing reviewer feedback. If I have to modify the code, I’ll mark my pull request as a draft first so as not to overwhelm people who have already reviewed it. When I move it back to ‘ready’, it sends a GitHub notification to those reviewers so they can look at it again.

items.title: 如何高效评审代码
items.source:
### Be gracious

The expression, “You can catch more flies with honey than vinegar,” comes to mind. I want reviews on my pull requests, so I like to reply to comments on my pull requests—especially if I disagree with the reviewer. Even if I don’t write a reply to a review comment, I’ll often react with a 👍 to indicate I agree or a ❤ to say thank you.

I want reviewers to trust that their suggestions won’t be forgotten, so I keep them in the loop via comments. If I agree with their suggestion—to go further refactoring existing code, for example—I may say as much while also pushing back about making that change in the current pull request. When I address their feedback in a later pull request, I come back to provide a link and let the reviewer know their feedback didn’t go unheard.

I’ll also tag them in later pull requests where I implement the suggested changes and include a note saying “This addresses @so-and-so’s feedback from <previous pull request URL>.” This both provides context for other readers and acts as a shout-out to the original reviewer, giving them credit for the idea.

When you follow through on a promise to address feedback in a later branch, that helps build trust with your reviewer, which can help them feel comfortable approving your future pull requests because they know that you won’t leave something incomplete.

## Wrap-up

Code review’s importance for product quality can’t be overstated, especially in the age of AI code generation. Many times in my career, a bug has been caught or an incident avoided simply by having that second set of eyes. Code review is well worth the time investment, whether spent in daily reviews, in ironing out processes, or in building automation to support it. It’s faster and less painful for developers to review pull requests thoroughly now than to deal with a problem later that’s already shipped to production.

Thank you for caring enough about code quality to read my philosophy on code review. Have you checked your review queue lately? Maybe now is a good time to put these ideas into action.

## Code Review Essentials for Software Teams

09 Feb 2015

Code Review is an essential part of any collaborative software
project. Large software systems are usually written by more than one
person, and so a highly functioning software team needs a robust
process to keep its members, as well as the code base itself moving in
the right direction.

Code Review is a powerful tool that:

- Helps team members adapt their mental model of the system as it’s
changing

- Ensures the change correctly solves the problem

- Opens discussion for strengths and weaknesses of a design

- Catches bugs before they get to production

- Keeps the code style and organization consistent

It’s helpful to think of these benefits as a hierarchy of
needs.

items.title: 代码评审要点
items.source:
## Keeping Team Members Together

The most critical function of a Code Review is to keep every member of
the team moving in the right direction. You can’t safetly change a
system you don’t understand, and so Code Review keeps the team
mentally aligned together. When Bob submits a pull request for the
accounting subsystem, Amy keeps her mental model of that system
updated as she reviews Bob’s code. Amy gets the chance to ask
questions about pieces she doesn’t understand, and Bob gets the
benefit of clarifying his design decisions as well as teaching someone
else about his work. When Amy has to make a change to the accounting
subsystem a month later, her mental model of the system is already up
to date and ready for action. She spends less time reading code and
trying to piece the system together in her brain, and more time
thinking about higher level abstractions and designs. Everyone wins,
because everyone stays together.

items.title: 代码评审要点
items.source:
## Executing a Good Pull Request

Before you even write a line of code changing the system, ask yourself the following
questions:

- “Is this the right thing to be working on?” There will always be
 competing needs from customers, internal team members and other
 parties. This can be a good way to keep priorities straight in your
 head before you dive in deep. Other processes like iteration /
 sprint planning meetings also help keep this on track.

- “Does the team already agree that the change is the right one?” If
not, it’d be better to start a design discussion by email or maybe
in person. Your changes are more likely to get accepted when people
are in agreement about the design before you change it.

- “How can I break this change into digestable chunks that are easy to
review and understand?” Small changes are easier to think about and
understand. Good discussions flow from the team being able to
comprehend your change quickly. If your change is massive,
teammate’s eyes will glaze over, and you might only get a few style
nitpicks from them.

- “How am I going to test this change to kill bugs and ensure
correctness?” You might have a QA department, but it’s still your
job as the developer to ship quality working software. Easily
testable software is usually more decoupled, is broken into smaller
chunks, and easier to reason about. You need to have a testing plan
for all your changes.

I’ve found that answering these questions ahead of time has saved me a
lot of headache in the long run. The last thing you want to do is
spend days coding up a change only to have it rejected based on
fundamental design flaws or team disagreement. Or for your change to
get held up because no one can verify it for correctness. Again, the
goal is to change the system while keeping other team members up to
date with your changes. Asking yourself about how you’re going to
break your work into bite-sized chunks and test those chunks is
helpful on many fronts:

- It reduces risk

- It makes changes easier to reason about

- It pushes you towards a better design

You’d rather make many small, precise cuts with a scalpel than one
giant gash with a machete. I prefer scalpel driven developement in
most additive cases, and like to save the machete for when it’s time
to delete large blocks of dead code.

items.source:
## Sending the Pull Request

Ok, so you’ve gotten buy-in from the team that your changes are good,
and you’ve achieved the design you set out to build. What’s the most
effective way to actually send your pull request? You’ve been working
hard on your changes, and you want other members of your team to pay
attention to your pull request and give you fast feedback. How can you
do that?

Remember earlier when I said that the most important part of a code
review is to keep the team’s collective mental model well aligned?
Your other teammates are probably working on something completely
different than you, maybe in a completely different part of the
system. Their brains are in a completely different context, so you
must overcome this by giving them the helpful guidance they need to do
the review. This means writing a well-organized description of the
changes you made, why you made them and any other relevant information
they won’t get from just reading the code alone. Don’t make your
teammates do more mental work than they have to.

Let’s look at some good and bad examples of pull request descriptions:

Bad Example:

items.source:
If you’re the developer of this pull request, stop and put yourself in
your code reviewer’s shoes for a second. The title is vague, and
raises more questions than answers: Where is the memory bug? How
critical is this change? What was the bug that Bob and you talked
about earlier? What trouble did you have with the compiler? The
description doesn’t provide any helpful context about the problem, nor
does it provide any helpful description of your changes. If this pull
request is long, the reviewer is going to have to dive into the code
and do mental gymnastics in an attempt to gain context before even
getting a chance to think about how this change fits in to the
coherent design of the system.

Here’s a improved example that helps clarify the changeset:

items.title: 代码评审要点
items.source:
A few things that have improved in this pull request description: The
title is descriptive enough to give the reviewer some short context,
and entice them to click on the email and learn more. The reviewer
knows it’s a process crash (which is usually a really bad thing) and
there’s also a bug report number where the reviewer can read more
details about the bug report if they’re interested in understand more
about the problem. The new description also outlines where the problem
was occuring, and helps give some context about how critical the fix
is. There’s a summary that lists the high level structural changes in
the pull request, which will give the reviewer a mental picture of the
changes before they even look at the code. Code reviewers should not
be surprised with what they find. This example also outlines testing
that was performed, which will give reviewers confidence that the
changes were well thought out, well tested and ready to be merged. Set
your reviewers up for success by making it stupid easy for them to
click ‘merge’.

items.title: 代码评审要点
items.source:
## Reviewers: Giving Constructive Feedback

The next part of the review process to consider is giving constructive
feedback to your peers. If the goal is clarity and alignment, giving
quality constructive feedback helps everyone understand the system
better and push towards better code.

Avoid saying things like:

- “This design is broken.” Why is it broken? How can it be made
 better? Statements like this hurt confidence and can bruise egos.

- “I don’t like this change.” Why don’t you like it? What would you
 like instead? It’s okay to not like something, but you should
 articulate your thoughts and provide helpful clues about how the
 code can be improved.

- “Can you rewrite this to be more clear?” What’s wrong with what
 I have now? How should I rewrite it? What’s unclear? Comments
 like this are themselves unclear, and don’t give a simple path
 forward.

Instead, say things like:

- “How does this code handle negative integers?” This feedback is
 specific, and causes the developer to think through the outcomes
 themselves. As a reviewer, you might know that the code in
 question crashes with negative integers, but it’s better to have
 the developer intuit this themselves. Questions like this might
 also be indicative of a testing gap, or a need for further
 specification of scope.

- “This section is confusing to me, I don’t understand why class A
 is talking to class B” If the developer hasn’t provided a helpful
 description, and the code isn’t neatly structured, this kind of
 comment helps drive for clarity of design and cleaner code.

- “It looks like you broke an interface boundary here. How will
 that affect the user?” You’ve pointed out an issue you noticed,
 giving them the benefit of the doubt that they meant to do it. Now
 they can think through the unseen ramifications of breaking the
 interface boundary and either provide a rationale for their
 decision, or choose to change it.

In general, framing feedback as questions is a good way to drive for
clarity, correctness, and at the same time help the developer improve
their designs in the future. This is usually how quality creative
writing groups give each other feedback. In a creative writing
setting, it’s harmful to say things like, “I don’t like this
character.” whereas the same comment can be reframed more clearly: “In
chapter one your character was warm and compassionate and now he’s
cold and icey. He doesn’t seem like a real person to me.” Now there’s
specific feedback that can be clarified to suss out the problem.

items.title: 代码评审要点
items.source:
Programmers like to solve problems and point out issues, so by nature
they like to discover and point out flaws. It’s tempting to see code
reviews as a way to prove how smart you are by finding problems in
your peer’s code. Don’t do it. Code review is a way to get more eyes
on a change and suss out critical problems, but your goal should be to
review in a way that encourages your team members to improve their
skills while fixing the problems at hand.

items.title: 代码评审要点
items.source:
## Style Points

Brace positions, variable / function names, indentation and spacing
issues should be addressed, but they are not the central purpose of
good code review (notice that I put them at the top the code
review pyramid). If you find that your team is spending 90% of it’s
time nitpicking indentation and variable names, you’re probably
wasting everyone’s time on something that could be mostly automated.
Write up a style guide, enforce indentation and spacing issues on
check-in and spend your time focusing on higher value issues. I don’t
want to diminish the importance of a consistent style. On the
contrary, having a consistent idiomatic style is one of the easiest
ways to make your codebase easy to read and comprehend. Still, if you
spend all of your code review focused on these simplistic tasks, ask
yourself whether you’re avoiding the harder and more important work of
keeping your team mentally aligned and thinking about higher level
designs.

# 如何高效评审代码：一位 GitHub 资深工程师的哲学

GitHub 资深工程师 Sarah Vessels 讲述了她对代码评审的哲学、好的代码评审与坏的代码评审之间的差别、她寻找和评审代码的策略，以及如何让别人评审自己的代码时收获最大。

Sarah Vessels·@cheshire137

2024 年 7 月 23 日
 

 |
 
 16 分钟

- 分享：

作为 GitHub 的一名资深工程师，代码评审是我日常工作的主要重心之一。过去八年里，我评审过 7,000 多个拉取请求。为什么会这么多？因为代码评审对构建优质软件至关重要，而多一双眼睛往往能发现你本来会错过的问题。

我把代码评审视为我工作中最重要的方面之一。事实上，每当我看到某位同事有一个准备好接受代码评审的拉取请求，我都更愿意放下自己正在处理的分支，去评审他们提议的改动。毕竟，他们的拉取请求已经通过了持续集成（CI）的连环考验，也达到了他们自己判断“做完”的标准，所以它大概比我手上还在进行的工作更接近可发布状态。我宁愿让他们的代码先冲过终点线，也不想再耗上不知多久去完成我自己的代码。

我给出反馈越早——“这里可能是 nil，会导致错误”“这看起来是个 n+1 查询”“这里最好有一个方法签名”——这些反馈就能被处理得越快，bug 就能被越早压掉、功能就能被越早发布。

我想分享一下我做代码评审的方式，希望我们都能发布更好的代码。
translations.how-to-review-code-effectively#0002:
## 什么是代码评审？

严格来说，代码评审——也就是 GitHub 上的拉取请求评审——让协作者能够对拉取请求中提出的改动发表评论，表示对这些改动的认可，或者在拉取请求被合并之前要求进一步修改。

我把拉取请求看作一段对话的开端。我读它的时候，等于作者在说“我觉得这比我们今天现有的东西更好”。代码评审是一次塑造产品实现方式的绝佳机会。作为代码评审者，我的工作就是通过提问、质疑假设，以及总体上充当第二双眼睛，与作者反复讨论，把他们的代码改得更好。

为什么要评审代码？这对你的职业生涯有好处

我从其他评审者对我自己代码的视角中学到了很多，而在反复收到“谢谢你及时做代码评审”这类正面反馈之后，我知道我的代码评审评论同样帮助队友们提升了自己。简单说，代码评审是有影响力的，而想升职就需要展示你的影响力。

代码评审之所以有影响力，是因为它促进知识共享并提升交付速度。它们是漂亮、可链接的产物，同事和主管可以拿它们来展示你有多乐于助人、多有见识。它们能凸显你良好的沟通能力，尤其是在需要处理复杂或有争议的改动时。所以，在代码评审中把自己的理由讲清楚，不仅能引导产品的未来、帮助避免故障事件，对你的职业生涯也有好处。

## 精细打磨你的代码评审流程
translations.how-to-review-code-effectively#0003:
### 如何找到待评审的拉取请求

我待在 GitHub 通知收件箱里。它是我在浏览器里固定仅有的几个标签页之一，所以随时都能打开。每当我在等 CI、在任务之间、开始一天工作，或者总之有点空闲时，我都喜欢去翻收件箱。我评审的大部分拉取请求都是在那里找到的。GitHub 的团队通常会有一个把某个 Slack 频道当作“大本营”，那是分享待评审拉取请求的好地方——这也是我发现拉取请求的另一条主要途径。

我还很好运地用起了 GitHub 的 Slack 集成，让某个 Slack 频道订阅与我团队相关的新拉取请求。为了过滤出哪些拉取请求出现在 Slack 里，我会用一个团队专属的标签，然后在 Slack 里输入一条类似 /github subscribe your/repo pulls +label:"your-team-label" 的‘subscribe’命令。

提示

你可以在查询中重复使用 team-review-requested: 这个限定符，从而拿到归属于许多不同代码归属方的待评审拉取请求。

我喜欢用 is:open archived:false is:pr org:github -is:draft team-review-requested:github/relevant-codeowner-team 这样的查询来搜索可能需要评审的未处理拉取请求。用这条查询，我能找到 GitHub 组织内开放的、未归档的、非草稿的拉取请求，并且它们把相关的代码归属团队列为请求的评审者。我通常会省略 review:required 这个搜索限定符，因为即使同事已经评审过某个拉取请求，我仍然想去评审它。毕竟，评审代码不仅能帮到作者，也能让我及时掌握影响到我负责代码的改动。
translations.how-to-review-code-effectively#0004:
### 用评审者团队管理通知

你不会希望代码改动去 ping 一个这么大的团队，以至于团队里的每个人都认为评审这个改动不是自己的责任。那会导致拉取请求要么一直没人评审、搁在那里，要么在该合并之前就被合并了——因为关键评审者在铺天盖地的通知里错过了它们。这两种情况都会影响产品质量。

如果做得到，我建议把自己所在的代码归属团队数量控制好，让通知保持在你可管理的范围内。这样，落到你收件箱里的拉取请求就不只是噪音，而是你真的觉得应该去评审的东西。大而全的代码归属团队作为兜底选项也许还行，但作为自动评审请求的第一线默认选项并不好。把仓库的 CODEOWNERS 文件组织好，配上界限清晰的代码划分，以限制通知量并帮助评审者避免通知疲劳。

限制团队通知的另一种办法，是建一个第一响应者团队，然后用自动化按排期增删团队成员。这样你的团队可以专注自己日常的代码库，而排班的第一响应者会收到你团队服务范围内拉取请求的通知。比如用 PagerDuty API，你可以确定某一天由谁担任第一响应者，然后用 Octokit 库来增删团队成员。
translations.how-to-review-code-effectively#0005:
### 用自动化让各团队的代码评审标准化

仓库级别的配置和自动化手段，比如使用 CODEOWNERS 文件和分支保护规则，有助于在各团队之间强制推行评审流程的标准。另一些标准，比如拉取请求中什么值得评论，就得由我们人类来维护。把团队内部的代码评审方式文档化下来，确保任何提供代码评审或提交拉取请求的人都知道，怎样让自己的拉取请求被评审、评审的预期周转时间是多少，以及有哪些自动化工具在辅助评审。

有些团队用项目看板来跟踪哪些拉取请求进来待评审；我见过一个管理共享 API 的团队这样做效果不错，因为这个区域经常被团队之外的人改动。另一些团队则只依赖 GitHub 通知，当代码归属划分得很紧、团队又自律地做到拉取请求一来就评审时，我也见过这种做法效果不错。

如果你遵循的是本团队特有的流程，自动化可以帮助你把预期传达给团队之外的人。例如，如果很多其他团队都依赖你团队的评审，你可以用一个机器人，在任何请求你团队评审的拉取请求上自动留一条评论，告诉作者大概什么时候能收到你的反馈。
translations.how-to-review-code-effectively#0006:
## 什么样的代码评审算好，什么样的算差

好的代码评审能增加清晰度，并把代码推向比起点更好的状态。

作为评审者，沟通上的清晰是关键。你需要说清楚哪些评论只是个人偏好，哪些是会卡住通过的阻塞项。给出你所建议做法的示例，能提升你这次代码评审的水平，也让你的意思更清楚。如果你能举一个来自该拉取请求所在同一个仓库的例子，那就更好了——这会以一致的实现方式进一步支撑你的建议。

相比之下，糟糕的代码评审缺乏清晰度。比如，不带任何评论就一律通过或一律拒绝，会让拉取请求的作者怀疑这次评审到底彻不彻底。即使只是在附上通过的同时重述一遍你对作者意图的理解，也能暴露出你和作者的理解是否一致。

没有说清建议应该在什么时候落实的代码评审，对作者来说也可能是糟糕的体验。指出已有的、未被改动的代码应该重构、或者应该多处理一种情况，这本身没问题，但重要的是要说明这些是否属于通过的前置条件。如果这个拉取请求没有你的建议也能落地，一定要说清楚。把差异保持得很小、把那些改动拆成单独的拉取请求分别发布，可能更稳妥。

下面这条代码评审评论既具体，又清楚传达了建议的实现方式：

“我看到你新增的方法和这个文件里现有的风格一致，接收 [X] 个参数。这么多参数会损害可读性，也暗示这个函数干了太多事。你怎么看：在后续的拉取请求里把这个方法和现有的那些方法一起重构一下，让它们接受的参数更少？”

这条评论好在哪里：

- 提供了具体细节。

- 指向了具体的代码或问题。

- 提出了问题的解决方案。

- 引用了证据或给出了解释

在光谱的另一端，下面这些评审评论就差点意思：

“我不喜欢这个。”——评审者不喜欢什么？他们心里有没有一个可以明说出来的替代方案？
translations.how-to-review-code-effectively#0007:
可以改进的地方：

- “这一行干的活儿太多了，能不能简化一下以提升可读性？”

- “我觉得这会有性能问题，因为它是个 n+1 查询。”

- “这个能不能改用 [preferred framework] 的现成方案，而不是自己写一套实现？”

“这样不行。”——为什么这些改动不行？

可以改进的地方：

- “这样不行，因为 [X]，参见这个相关 issue：[issue link]。”

- “这个在 [pull request link] 里已经试过了，因为 [X] 所以行不通。”

- “如果你在 [X] 上遇到问题，可以试试 [alternative approach]。”

“我觉得这修掉了一个 bug。”——我很喜欢这种点明，但有没有额外的上下文，比如一个 issue 链接，能让这句话更清楚？

可以改进的地方：

- “我觉得这修的是 [issue link] 里的问题。”

- “这是在修 [issue link] 里的那个 bug 吗？”

- “这看起来就是我们在 [link to failing build] 时遇到的那个问题。谢谢修复！”
translations.how-to-review-code-effectively#0008: ## 如何给出好的代码评审
translations.how-to-review-code-effectively#0009:
### 多提问

我把拉取请求的作者视为对这次改动最了解的人。我可以基于自己的经历——在 Ruby on Rails 单体应用、TypeScript，或者大流量数据库上工作的经验——指出我看到的问题，但我信任作者对我问题的回答。我认为他们对这些细节的理解比我的更可靠。

提示

如果你刚加入一个代码库或团队，就在代码评审中多提问，以此了解技术栈以及有哪些内部工具和库可用。你评审的每一个拉取请求，都是一次弄清作者为什么偏好这个做法而不是另一个的机会。

我还很喜欢问那些涉及代码中所做假设的问题。他们处理的数据是什么形状？是否存在与该形状不匹配的数据？代码对此应对得好吗？这段代码资源消耗大吗？性能会好吗？作为评审者，我最喜欢的回答是作者提供一个自动化测试，验证这些场景下的行为。我第二喜欢的回答是实测数据，比如从我们的数据仓库跑出来的一个查询，或者一张 Datadog 图表，说明这些场景不是问题。

作为拉取请求的作者，我很看重有人提问。当有人提问时，就给了我空间去解释我为什么对自己的改动有信心，必要时可以引用 issue、查询或图表。这也让我能把知识和经验分享给别人。作者看到的不仅是我的回答，还有其他评审者，以及日后可能需要追溯某个过往决定背景的读者。
translations.how-to-review-code-effectively#0010:
### 给出肯定

除了提问之外，对拉取请求中你认同的部分发表评论也是个好习惯。这类评论能表明你确实读了并理解所做的改动，或者你验证了代码里的某个假设。举几个例子：

- “看起来这和这个模块里其他类用的模式一致。”

- “谢谢你为这个补了测试！”

- “这比之前可读性好多了。”

以我的经验，能收到这样的评论感觉也很好。接收一次代码评审有时会让人感到被消耗。当我同时应付好几个人提出的问题和建议时，能收到几条不要求我做任何事、而是支持并认可我已经投入的工作的评论，会很提气。
translations.how-to-review-code-effectively#0011:
### 留意偏见和假设

你很容易让自己对评审者的偏见、或对他们所改的那块代码的偏见，影响你的评审。你会习惯某个人一直在某个领域工作、或有某种资历，于是假设他们知道自己在干什么——但每个人都会犯错。用你的眼睛去看他们的改动、用你的问题去检验他们的假设或验证你自己的假设，能在问题被部署之前抓住它。

我非常推崇写测试，因为测试能消掉一部分偏见。当你写一个测试来检查代码是否正常工作，你不必只凭作者的一面之辞，只要看测试有没有通过就行——当然，前提是这个测试本身写得对。😅

我也非常支持初级开发者在代码评审中向资深开发者提问，即使他们觉得自己的问题很傻、或答案显而易见。如果对你来说它并不明显，那这个提问就是合理的。对别人来说它也不会明显！把问题问出来，给作者留出写下答案的空间，把这份知识留给后来的人。
translations.how-to-review-code-effectively#0012:
### 批还是不批

我把自己的评审看作一道会挡住别人的闸门——它可能阻止某个人改进我们的产品——所以我会谨慎地不予通过。我常常有自己的个人偏好，会建议一些我希望作者能做的可选改动，但不会仅凭这些就扣住不给通过。如果我对某人的拉取请求有建议，但这个拉取请求按现状不会搞坏生产、不会对用户造成负面影响、也不会引发其他问题，我就会带着这些评论给出通过。作者可以选择在合并前处理我的反馈，也可以另开一个分支后续跟进。

提示

使用功能开关（feature flags），并把拉取请求做小。你的改动越不吓人，在生产上被回滚得就越快，我也就越容易批准它！

评审代码时，要掂量你那条建议的重要程度。为了让建议被采纳而推迟发布，值得吗？值得让作者经历一整轮流程——看到你的反馈、做出建议的修改、等待 CI、再次评审、部署，最后才合并吗？如果少了这条建议不会让谁的处境变差，那就让作者自己决定要不要改、什么时候改。

“Request changes”选项会阻止拉取请求被合并，直到评审者回来给出通过。我极少用它，因为通常感觉太粗暴了。我信任我的团队知道什么时候该批准一个拉取请求，所以同事的通过就可以代替我的通过。同样地，我信任拉取请求的作者会重视并考虑我的反馈，而不是因为别人批准了我没批准就盲目合并。我几乎只有在认为存在一个紧迫的安全问题时才会选“Request changes”——因为我担心他们合并前看不到我的顾虑。

使用 AI 编码工具时，代码评审为什么依然重要

AI 编码工具通常包含各种防止代码出错或不安全的防护措施，但别被这种虚假的安全感哄睡。作为掌舵的人类评审者，你是最后一道防线，应该以同等严谨的态度评审所有代码。

## 如何让代码评审发挥最大价值
translations.how-to-review-code-effectively#0013:
### 评审你自己的代码

GitHub 资深软件工程师 Paul Smith 教过我，在请别人评审之前先评审自己的拉取请求，我也建议你这么做。先过一遍，对那些不明显的改动——或者你在别人的拉取请求里看到会想问一句的改动——用行内评论的方式标出来。自我评审还能帮你判断一个拉取请求是不是太大了、拆开会更好。

特别推荐：如果你在意让拉取请求保持小规模，可以用 lerebear/sizeup-action 自动给拉取请求打上标签，标明其复杂度和规模。
translations.how-to-review-code-effectively#0014:
### 欢迎合并之后的评审

如果我碰巧在别人有机会评审之前就合并了拉取请求，我依然欢迎他们的评审。如果我的拉取请求弄坏了什么、或者带来了意料之外的后果，那就在拉取请求上尽量多留评论，让这些面包屑小径帮助日后的读者追查当时发生了什么！

如果我收到针对已合并拉取请求的评审，我会像它还没落地时那样处理这些反馈。可能是一条评论解释我的思路，也可能是再开几个拉取请求来迭代我最初发布的代码，还可能是开几个新 issue 来记录待做的额外工作。
translations.how-to-review-code-effectively#0015:
### 使用草稿拉取请求

创建新拉取请求时，你可以选择把拉取请求设为草稿。我非常依赖草稿状态来表示我要不要接受评审。比如，如果某个必需的 CI 构建挂了，或者我还没写完，我就把它保持为草稿。我对别人的拉取请求也有同样的预期：如果是草稿，我就认为作者还没准备好接受评审；如果被标记为准备接受评审，我就认为只要拿到足够多的通过，就能发布了。

草稿状态意味着拉取请求还没完成，所以我在解决合并冲突或处理评审反馈时，会把拉取请求退回草稿状态。如果我必须修改代码，我会先把自己的拉取请求标为草稿，以免把已经评审过的人淹掉。当我把它改回‘准备好’时，GitHub 会给这些评审者发通知，让他们可以再去看一遍。
translations.how-to-review-code-effectively#0016:
### 保持善意

我总想起那句话：“用蜂蜜比用醋能招来更多苍蝇。”我希望我的拉取请求能得到评审，所以有人在我的拉取请求上评论时，我总愿意回复——尤其是在我不同意评审者意见的时候。即使我没有对某条评审评论写出回复，我也常用一个 👍 表示我同意，或者用一个 ❤ 表示感谢。

我希望评审者相信他们的建议不会被忘记，所以我用评论让他们一直知情。如果我认同他们的建议——比如建议进一步重构现有代码——我可能会表示认同，同时又提出这个改动不该放在当前这个拉取请求里。当我在后续的拉取请求里处理了他们的反馈时，我会回来附上链接，让评审者知道他们的反馈没有被忽略。

我也会在落实这些建议的后续拉取请求里 @ 上他们，并加一句说明：“这条处理了 @某某 在 <previous pull request URL> 提出的反馈。”这既为其他读者提供了上下文，也是对最初评审者的一次致意，把这个想法的功劳归给他们。

当你兑现承诺、在后续分支里处理了反馈时，这有助于建立评审者对你的信任，也能让他们更自在地批准你以后的拉取请求，因为他们知道你不会把事情留在半途。

代码评审对产品质量的重要性怎么强调都不为过，在 AI 生成代码的时代尤其如此。在我的职业生涯中有很多次，只是因为多了那一双眼睛，就抓住了一个 bug 或避免了一场故障事件。无论时间花在每天的评审上、花在梳理流程上，还是花在构建支撑评审的自动化上，代码评审都完全值得这份投入。让开发者现在把拉取请求彻底评审一遍，比事后去处理一个已经发布到生产的问题要更快、也没那么痛苦。

### 了解 AI 代码评审

AI 代码评审是指利用机器学习和自然语言处理技术，自动分析代码中的问题，包括：

- Bug 和潜在的运行时错误

- 性能低效

与传统的静态分析工具不同，现代 AI 代码评审工具能够理解代码上下文、提出改进建议，甚至自动生成修复方案。

- 效率更高——自动化缩短了评审时间，并提前发现问题

- 更一致——AI 在所有代码评审中套用同一套标准

- 知识共享——开发者通过 AI 的建议学到最佳实践

- 更低的认知负担——AI 处理常规检查，让人专注复杂逻辑

### 常见问题
translations.ai-code-review-best-practices#0018:
#### AI 代码评审工具有多准？

对于语法错误、风格违规和基本安全漏洞这类常见问题，AI 代码评审工具的准确率通常在 70%–90%。不过，准确率会随问题的复杂度和具体工具而显著变化。对于架构决策和复杂业务逻辑，人工评审依然不可替代。
translations.ai-code-review-best-practices#0019:
#### AI 代码评审能完全取代人类评审者吗？

不能，AI 代码评审应当是人类评审者的补充，而不是替代。AI 擅长发现例行问题并保持一致性，但在架构决策、业务逻辑验证和复杂问题求解上，仍然需要人类评审者。最有效的做法是把 AI 自动化与人类专业能力结合起来。
translations.ai-code-review-best-practices#0020:
#### 我怎么说服团队采用 AI 代码评审？

先从有热情的团队成员参与的小范围试点开始。用节省下来的时间、变好的代码质量指标和下降的 bug 率来展示明确的价值。至于对岗位安全的顾虑，就把 AI 定位成一个效率工具，让开发者能专注更高价值的工作。
translations.ai-code-review-best-practices#0021:
#### 我该怎么处理 AI 代码评审带来的误报？

建立一个反馈闭环，让开发者可以把建议标记为误报。大多数工具都允许你调节灵敏度设置，并为特定代码模式创建忽略规则。定期复盘误报，有助于随时间推移提升系统的准确率。
translations.ai-code-review-best-practices#0022:
#### 使用 AI 代码评审工具时，我的代码安全吗？

安全性取决于工具和部署模式。基于云的工具可能在外部服务器上处理你的代码，而本地部署方案则把代码留在你自己的基础设施内。选择方案时，请审查每个工具的数据处理政策，并结合你组织的安全要求来考虑。

#### AI 代码评审会拖慢我的开发流程吗？

一开始可能会有一点学习曲线，但大多数团队在 2-4 周内就能看到整体时间上的节省。AI 早早发现问题，减少了调试时间和评审轮次。关键在于合理配置，让它聚焦高影响的问题，而不是用一堆细枝末节的建议淹没开发者。
translations.ai-code-review-best-practices#0024:
#### 我该如何把 AI 代码评审接入现有的 CI/CD 流水线？

大多数 AI 代码评审工具都提供 API 集成和 webhook 支持。你通常可以把它作为 CI 流水线中的一个步骤，或作为拉取请求上的自动化检查来接进来。先从基础集成开始，随着团队逐渐适应，再逐步加入更复杂的工作流。
translations.ai-code-review-best-practices#0025:
#### 我该如何平衡 AI 的建议与团队的编码规范？

把 AI 工具配置成与现有的编码规范和风格指南一致。大多数工具都允许定制规则，也能从你的代码库模式中学习。要根据团队反馈和不断演进的标准，定期复审并调整配置。
translations.ai-code-review-best-practices#0026:
#### 我该如何衡量 AI 代码评审实现的成效？

跟踪这些指标：生产 bug 的减少量、代码评审节省下来的时间、开发者满意度评分，以及代码质量的改善。落地前先建立基线测量，使用 3-6 个月后再对比结果。
translations.ai-code-review-best-practices#0027:
#### AI 漏掉了人类评审能发现的重要问题，该怎么改进？

这很常见，也在预期之内。AI 工具擅长模式识别，但可能漏掉与具体上下文相关的问题。要用人类监督来补上 AI 评审，尤其是复杂逻辑和架构决策部分。利用 AI 反馈来改进工具配置，并为领域特定的模式考虑自定义规则。

## 软件团队的代码评审要点

2015 年 2 月 9 日

代码评审是任何协作式软件
项目中不可或缺的一部分。大型软件系统通常由不止一个人
编写，因此一个高效运转的软件团队需要一套稳健的
流程，让成员以及代码库本身都朝着正确的方向前进。

代码评审是一件强大的工具，它：

- 帮助团队成员随着系统
的变化调整自己的心智模型

- 确保改动正确地解决了问题

- 为设计的优点和缺点打开讨论

- 在 bug 进入生产之前抓住它们

- 让代码风格和组织结构保持一致

把这些收益看成一组层次递进的需求会很有帮助。
translations.code-review-essentials#0002:
## 让团队成员保持在同一条船上

代码评审最关键的作用，是让团队里的每一位成员
都朝着正确的方向前进。你无法安全地改动一个
你不理解的系统，所以代码评审让团队在心智上
保持同步。当 Bob 为记账子系统提交一个拉取请求时，
Amy 会在评审 Bob 代码的过程中持续更新自己对该
系统的理解。Amy 有机会对自己不理解的部分提问，
而 Bob 既能借此讲清自己的设计决策，也能把
自己的工作讲给别人听。一个月后，当 Amy
要改动记账子系统时，她对这个系统的理解
已经是最新的，可以直接动手。她花在读代码、
在脑海里拼凑系统上的时间更少，花在思考
更高层抽象与设计上的时间更多了。所有人都赢，
因为所有人都保持在同一条船上。
translations.code-review-essentials#0003:
## 执行一个好的拉取请求

在你为改动系统写第一行代码之前，先问问自己以下
问题：

- “这是应该做的那件事吗？” 客户、内部团队成员和其他
 各方的需求永远在互相竞争。在一头扎进去之前，这
 是一个让你在脑子里理清优先级的好办法。迭代 /
 冲刺计划会议之类的其他流程也有助于让这件事
 保持在正轨上。

- “团队是否已经一致认为这个改动是对的？” 如果
 没有，那最好先通过邮件或者当面开启一场设计讨论。
 人们在你动手之前就已经对设计达成一致，你的改动
 才更有可能被接受。

- “我怎样把这次改动拆成容易评审和理解的小块？”
 小改动更容易思考和理解。好的讨论来自团队能够
 快速理解你的改动。如果你的改动非常庞大，
 队友的眼睛会看得发直，你可能只会从他们那里
 得到几条吹毛求疵的风格意见。

- “我打算怎样测试这个改动，以消灭 bug 并确保
 正确性？” 你也许有 QA 部门，但把高质量、能用的软件
 交付出去，仍然是作为开发者的你的职责。容易
 测试的软件通常耦合更低、拆成了更小的
 块，也更容易推理。你需要为所有改动
 准备一份测试计划。

我发现提前回答这些问题从长远来看替我省去了
大量麻烦。你最不希望发生的，就是花几天时间把一个
改动写出来，最后却因为根本性的设计缺陷或团队分歧
而被否掉。或者你的改动因为没人能验证其正确性而
被卡住。再说一次，目标是在改动系统的同时让其他
团队成员了解你的改动。问问自己打算怎样把工作
拆成一口口能吃下的小块并对这些小块做测试，在很多
方面都有好处：

- 它降低风险

- 它让改动更容易推理

- 它推动你做出更好的设计

与其用砍刀划出一道长伤口，你更愿意用手术刀
做出许多小而精准的切口。多数增量式的场景我都更偏好
手术刀式的开发，而把砍刀留到该删除大块死代码的时候。

## 发送拉取请求

好，团队已经认可你的改动，你的目标设计也已经
实现了。那么，怎样才是真正把你的拉取请求发出去的
最有效方式？你在改动上花了很大力气，你希望团队里
的其他成员关注你的拉取请求，并给你快速反馈。你该
怎么做？

还记得我之前说过，代码评审最重要的部分，是让
团队的整体心智模型保持良好一致吗？你的其他队友
很可能在忙完全不同的事，也许在系统里完全不同的
一部分。他们的大脑处在完全不同的上下文中，所以
你必须给他们做好评审所需的有益指引，来弥补这一点。
这意味着要条理清晰地写清你做了哪些改动、为什么
这么做，以及其他光读代码得不到的相关信息。不要
让你的队友做超出必要范围的脑力活。

## 评审者：给出建设性反馈

评审流程中接下来要考虑的，是给同伴
建设性反馈。如果目标是清晰和一致，那么给出
高质量的建设性反馈能帮助所有人更好地理解系统，
并推动代码变得更好。

避免说这样的话：

- “这个设计是坏的。” 它坏在哪里？怎么才能改好？
 这类说法会打击信心、伤害自尊。

- “我不喜欢这个改动。” 你为什么不喜欢？你希望
 它变成什么样？不喜欢某样东西没关系，但你应该
 把自己的想法讲清楚，并给出代码可以如何改进的
 有益线索。

- “你能把这个重写得更清楚一点吗？” 我现在这版
 有什么问题？该怎么重写？哪里不清楚？这类
 评论本身就不清楚，也没给出一条简单的
 前进路径。

改成说这样的话：

- “这段代码怎么处理负整数？” 这条反馈很具体，
 会促使开发者自己去推演结果。作为评审者，你可能
 知道这段代码遇到负整数会崩溃，但让开发者
 自己领悟到更好。这类问题也可能意味着测试
 覆盖不足，或者需要进一步明确范围。

- “这一部分让我看不明白，我不理解为什么类 A 要和类 B
 通信” 如果开发者没有提供有帮助的描述、
 代码结构也不够清晰，这类评论能推动设计
 变得更清楚、代码变得更干净。

- “看起来你在这里破坏了一个接口边界。这会怎么
 影响用户？” 你指出了一个注意到的问题，同时
 善意地相信他是有意为之。现在他可以权衡破坏
 接口边界那些看不见的后果，然后要么为
 自己的决定给出理由，要么选择改掉。

总的来说，把反馈包装成问题是推动清晰和
正确性的好办法，同时也能帮助开发者日后
改进自己的设计。优秀的创作型写作小组通常
就是这样互相给反馈的。在写作的场合下，说“我不喜欢
这个人物”是有害的，而同样的意见换个说法可以更清楚：
“第一章里你的人物温暖又体贴，现在他
冷漠又冰冷。在我看来他不像个真人。”这样就有了
具体的反馈，可以进一步追问、把问题弄清楚。
translations.code-review-essentials#0010:
程序员喜欢解决问题、指出问题，所以从本性上
说，他们喜欢发现并指出缺陷。很容易把代码
评审当成一种证明自己有多聪明的办法——在
同伴的代码里找出问题。别这么做。代码评审是
让一次改动多几双眼睛、把关键问题揪出来的方式，
但你的目标应该是以一种能鼓励团队成员在修复
手头问题的同时提升自己技能的方式去做评审。
translations.code-review-essentials#0011:
## 风格问题

大括号位置、变量/函数命名、缩进和空格
问题应该处理，但它们不是好代码评审的核心目的
（注意我把它们放在了代码评审金字塔的最
上面）。如果你发现团队把 90% 的时间
花在挑缩进和变量名的毛病上，那你多半是在
把所有人的时间浪费在一件基本可以自动化的事情上。
写一份风格指南，在代码签入时就强制处理缩进和
空格问题，把时间花在更高价值的问题上。我并不想
贬低一致风格的重要性。恰恰相反，拥有
一致地道的风格，是让你的代码库易于阅读和理解
最省力的方式之一。不过，如果你把全部代码评审都
花在这些简单任务上，那要问问自己：是不是
在回避那些更难也更重要的——让团队在心智上保持一致、
思考更高层次设计的工作。
